verdict: Lend selectively to Tuticorin port-linked service and logistics borrowers with contracted volumes and clean receivables; avoid pure coal-handling and single-client stevedoring exposure until cargo mix and receivable data are verified.
title: Tuticorin Ports & Port Services: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Port services in Tuticorin convert vessel calls and cargo tonnage into fees for handling, storage, stevedoring, transport and terminal support.** The cash engine is throughput: every extra tonne handled pulls labour, equipment and working capital through the system. V.O.C. Port crossed the 25-million-tonne cargo mark in FY 2026–27 [1], and the port reports annual cargo-handling capacity of 82 mn t [2]. **Capacity is not the constraint; utilisation and cargo mix are.**

## Where value and cash sit
**Value sits in berth access, equipment utilisation and the receivable cycle, not in the asset base.** Peer rating work shows receivable periods of 60 days in FY25 (FY24: 52 days) for one port operator [8] and an operating cycle of 51 days in FY24 for a port group [9]. So when a proposal lands, check debtor days against these benchmarks; if receivables run past 60 days, ask which customer and what the collection history is. **Capex is heavy and lumpy** — the outer harbour alone is an investment of more than Rs. 150 bn and is planned to add 4 mn t per year of capacity [2]. Borrowers feeding that project carry execution risk, not demand risk.

## What has changed now
**Local news is positive on volume and green transition, but cost pressure is real.** TICT has been declared a green terminal after full electrification, with 13 electric internal transfer vehicles flagged off [2], and the port reviewed green projects worth more than Rs. 184 bn [2]. Against that, a peer-market report notes cost inflation partially offsetting volume expansion in logistics and ports in Q2FY27 [7]. Peer results are strong — Adani Ports reported Q2 FY27 profit up 16.5% to Rs 3,622 crore on revenue of Rs 11,340 crore, with EBITDA margin at 60% [5][6] — but that is a national operator, not a Tuticorin proxy. **Sources say little about Tuticorin's own service-layer margins; lean on first principles and peers.**

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue borrowers tied to container and green-terminal activity, and to the outer harbour build.** Target stevedoring and equipment-hire firms with multi-client contracts, CFS and transport operators serving TICT, and contractors with awarded outer-harbour packages [2]. Avoid single-client coal handlers and pure labour contractors with no equipment. Structure against contracted volumes, take monthly stock and debtor statements, and require a borrowing-base certificate. **Take every month: cargo handled, debtor ageing, and equipment utilisation.**

## Early-warning signs
- **Debtor days crossing 60 [8] (monthly)** -> ask for customer-wise ageing and stop fresh limits.
- **Cargo volume stalling below the 25-million-tonne run-rate [1] (monthly)** -> reprice or reduce exposure.
- **Cost inflation compressing margin without a tariff pass-through [7] (quarterly)** -> seek revised pricing evidence.
- **Delay in outer-harbour milestones [2] (quarterly)** -> review contractor cash flow.
